https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: Trees sway in high winds as the Eaton Fire burns in Altadena in January last year. Photograph: Ethan Swope/AP View image in fullscreen Trees sway in high winds as the Eaton Fire burns in Altadena in January last year. Photograph: Ethan Swope/AP Los Angeles Devastating LA wildfire sparked by utility company tower, long-awaited report finds Investigators pin blame for Eaton fire, which killed 19 people and ruined thousands of homes, on ‘electrical arcing events’ at out-of-service tower Associated Press Tue 4 Aug 2026 15.13 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The deadly 2025 Eaton fire in the Los Angeles area was caused by equipment belonging to the utility company Southern California Edison, fire officials said in a report released on Tuesday. Los Angeles county fire officials found that the cause of the fire that killed 19 people and destroyed or damaged more than 9,000 homes and businesses was a tower that was not in service, according to the report. “After 18 months of thorough review of all evidence, alongside retained electrical and metallurgical experts, the investigation concluded that the cause of the wildfire conflagration was due to the electrical arcing events that took place on the out-of-service Southern California Edison (SCE) tower,” the agency said in a statement. It took firefighters nearly a month to extinguish the blaze, which scorched 22 sq miles (57 sq km). View image in fullscreen The Eaton fire in Altadena in January 2025. Photograph: Josh Edelson/AFP/Getty Images Kathleen Dunleavy, a spokesperson for Southern California Edison, said the utility has received the report and is reviewing it. “We have taken our potential role in the start of this fire seriously from the very beginning,” Dunleavy said. She said SCE previously acknowledged “it was likely our equipment was associated with the ignition of the Eaton fire”. She said the utility continues to support the community as it recovers . SoCal Edison has claimed in lawsuits earlier this year that Los Angeles county agencies failed to send timely evacuation warnings to residents in east and west Altadena. Eighteen of the 19 people who died in the fire lived in west Altadena. The utility also has claimed water agencies, including Pasadena Water and Power, did not provide enough water as the fire spread, leaving firefighters with limited resources. Los Angeles county declined to comment about the latest court filings. The Los Angeles county arson fire investigation unit jointly conducted the investigation with California department of forestry and fire protection. It found electrical arcing on the utility’s out-of-service tower sparked the dry brush below and that the utility was responsible for maintaining and operating its electrical lines and equipment “in a manner that would minimize the risk of catastrophic wildfire posed by them.” Their homes burned in the LA wildfires. A year later, thousands still can’t return Read more The blaze was sparked during extreme weather conditions that included high temperatures, low humidity and powerful winds. Two “electrical arcing events” occurred in quick succession, causing an unknown burning material to fall from the tower to the ground below, according to the report. Within 12 seconds, dry grass and brush was ignited and the fire swiftly developed “into a conflagration engulfing the areas of the San Gabriel Mountains, Altadena, Pasadena, Sierra Madre and La Cañada Flintridge”, the report said. It took more than two weeks to fully contain the wildfire. The report cites an interview with a Pasadena resident who called 911 on 7 January after spotting flames across the canyon from his home’s rear window. The caller described it “as a 10in x 10in fire at the base of a high-voltage electrical tower”, the report said. The Eaton fire burned at the same time as the Palisades fire, the most destructive blaze in Los Angeles to date and among the five worst in California’s history. The blaze killed 12 people and destroyed more than 6,800 homes and buildings in Pacific Palisades. The fire ripped through hillside neighborhoods, destroying mansions with spectacular ocean views. The man accused of sparking the Palisades fire will be tried again this fall after his first federal arson case ended in a mistrial in June. Prosecutors said Jonathan Rinderknecht used a barbecue lighter on 1 January 2025 to spark a blaze that burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up 7 January. https://www.politico.eu/article/spain-ho.text: MADRID — Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez faces renewed pressure as housing protests in Madrid escalate and his left-wing allies demand tougher action, straining his coalition ahead of a key election year. Wheelchair-bound pensioner Maricarmen Abascal , 87, was forcibly removed from her home after living there since 1956, after failing to meet the new rental demands set by the investment firm that bought her building. Thousands marched through the capital on Saturday, with some protestors then pitching tents in the historic Puerto del Sol square. By Monday, hundreds of tents had been erected. “We live in a country full of Maricarmens, and we’re saying enough is enough,” said Valeria Racu, spokesperson for the Madrid Tenant Union, the group leading the encampment. During a speech to protesters on Sunday, thousands echoed a chant denouncing “ inversores culpables, gobierno responsable ,” meaning “guilty investors, responsible government” Advertisement Advertisement Sánchez, who last week called the eviction was a “social tragedy,” is now scrambling to contain the situation by vowing to approve a long-delayed housing bill at Tuesday’s meeting of Spain’s Council of Ministers. But crafting legislation that his minority government can get through parliament is proving tricky. The draft bill must be moderate enough to win the support of the Catalan separatist Junts party, which is conservative on landowners’ rights. But if the legislation is too lenient, Sánchez risks alienating his left-wing allies, accentuating his political isolation in a key election year. The beleaguered prime minister is already facing mounting pressure over the unresolved migrant crisis in Ceuta, as well as a slew of corruption scandals involving family members and close allies. According to Spanish newspaper El País, a version of the draft text under negotiation on Monday night proposed extending protections against evictions for vulnerable tenants through 2028, capping rent increases at 2 percent in certain cases and offering tax breaks to tenants in rent-stressed areas. Additional measures would seek to ban speculative home purchases by investment funds and potentially raise taxes on short-term tourist flats. Those proposals fall short of the ambitious action Sumar, the smaller partner in Sánchez’s coalition, is demanding. Deputy Prime Minister Yolanda Díaz on Monday called for the public to mobilize against her own government to ensure the draft bill is “up to task.” “In this country, rights don’t just fall from the sky,” she said. The current draft is also unlikely to satisfy the protesters occupying the square, who are demanding the legislation include the automatic renewal of rental contracts, tougher action against abusive landlords and a freeze on rents until the housing crisis is resolved. Advertisement Advertisement “We’re fed up with weak measures that do nothing to solve the problem,” said Jorge Collado, a 26-year-old student participating in the occupation. Collado said he had been forced to move back to his family’s home after his former landlord dramatically raised the monthly rent when he requested a legal rental contract. “This allegedly progressive government has spent the past eight years promising to do something about housing, but has systematically sided with the landlords who exploit us,” he said. Pedro Sánchez delivers a speech to MPs in the lower house of parliament in Madrid on June 24, 2026. | Oscar del Pozo/AFP via Getty Images With Spain due to hold national elections within the next year , Collado said the government would be making a big mistake if it didn’t take immediate steps to rectify the situation. “When election day comes, I think many people will stay home,” he said. “And in the meantime, we’ll be staying here, for as long as it takes.” Pablo Simón, a political scientist at Carlos III University of Madrid, called the protests “devastating” for Sánchez. Advertisement Advertisement “These demonstrations are channelling the broad dissatisfaction of left-wing voters who feel this government has failed to deliver on its progressive promises,” he said. “They’re opening a major breach in Sánchez’s strategy for political survival: If that electorate doesn’t show up, he’s doomed.” Marta García, a 60-year-old retired schoolteacher who was present at the anti-austerity 15-M protests in the same square about 15 years ago, said she had traveled from outside Madrid to support the protesters sleeping there. “This is an encampment founded on rage — rage at the shameless speculative practices, at the incompetent political maneuvers, at the squandered futures — but also on the hope that things can change and be made better,” she said. “A bill that fails, but is ambitious and courageous, will have much more of an impact than a toothless one that passes.”

http://www.russiaherald.com/news/2794101.text: Tusk's Kaliningrad gamble RT.com 04 Nov 2026, 02:38 GMT+10 The Polish PM has launched a counter-terror operation on Russia's border, while his government descends into infighting With a constitutional crisis tearing the Polish government apart, an anti-Russia "special operation" was just what Prime Minister Donald Tusk needed to reassert his power - but his gamble could spiral out of control with horrific consequences. Poland has sent extra police and counter-terror units to its border with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, Tusk announced on Tuesday, claiming that Warsaw had received reports that "acts of diversion or more serious provocations on the border with Russia, or even sabotage acts orchestrated by hostile services, could occur." "Having received more precise information that incidents could occur in the first half of November - including an incursion into Polish territory by armed individuals - we decided to deploy substantial police and counter-terrorism forces to the border and to strengthen the border guard," he said, claiming that Polish services had been tipped off by NATO, and by Ukrainian and American intelligence agencies, including the CIA. Tusk said that Polish border guards spotted "people with torches" on the Russian side of the border on Monday night, but offered no further evidence of a pending "incursion." What about that timing? Tusk is one of the EU's loudest proponents of the "hybrid war" theory - that Russia is waging an invisible, unprovable, yet very real war against Europe. Last month, he claimed that this supposed "hybrid war" would soon heat up, and that "we should expect... attempts at sabotage or some form of provocation in Poland" before Christmas, citing information from "Ukrainian security services and those of our allies." Russia has repeatedly described these claims as self-serving, with President Vladimir Putin noting last month that European leaders "desperately need to divert public attention away from domestic problems and towards external issues." As if to prove Putin's point, when nationalist protesters descended upon Poland's Constitutional Tribunal building after it was raided by police on Friday, Tusk was ready and waiting to pin the unrest on Moscow. The demonstrators were backed by "pro-Russian forces worldwide," he said in a televised address on Saturday, adding that "an army of Russian bots online" were cheering them on. In reality, Poland has been locked into an intra-elite power struggle for more than a decade, with the country's top court a key flashpoint. Tusk's liberal Civic Coalition controls Poland's parliament, while Nawrocki, a member of the right-wing PiS party, holds the presidency, and the Constitutional Tribunal is dominated by judges appointed by PiS before Tusk took power in 2023. During PiS' eight years in power, the EU repeatedly accused the party of manipulating the court, after it ruled in favor of Polish law over EU law on multiple occasions. With Nawrocki en-route to Senegal on a state visit on Friday, a faction of judges loyal to Tusk announced the suspension of the court's PiS-appointed president, Bogdan Swieczkowski, and the appointment of a Tusk loyalist. Nawrocki cut his trip short and returned to the court, where he declared that "the constitutional order of the Republic of Poland was violated and a constitutional body of state was forcibly seized." Tusk maintains that he took "decisive action" after "years of PiS-led lawlessness." The court's PiS-appointed justices accuse the PM of waging a judicial "coup d'etat." Negotiations between Tusk and Nawrocki have not yet managed to defuse the crisis. Nobody's buying it Tusk's attempt to blame the unrest outside the court on Russia fell flat. Thousands of protesters returned to the court on Tuesday as Tusk's appointee chaired an assembly without any PiS-loyal judges in attendance. Police surrounded the court building, with clubs, shields, and - according to Poland's Onet news site - "pain thrower" acoustic weapons ready to deploy should a riot break out. During a National Security Council meeting on Tuesday, Nawrocki declared that "full responsibility for every police officer in the Constitutional Tribunal, the suspension of judges, illegal orders, and the entry into the Tribunal rests with one man, present in this room... Prime Minister Donald Tusk." The Kaliningrad gambit In Poland, Tusk's announcement of the Kaliningrad operation has been widely derided on social media as an attempt to draw public attention away from the court showdown. However, whether this was his intention or not, Tusk's government has already been explicit that it intends to escalate tension with Russia along the 210 km Poland-Kaliningrad frontier. Polish troops have taken part in two separate rounds of NATO military exercises near the Kaliningrad border so far this year. In September, Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski suggested that NATO "exercise so aggressively" on the borders of the exclave, that Moscow would be left "uncertain of what we will do." Uncertainty, however, carries immense risks. After Sikorski's comments, and following repeated threats by Lithuania to blockade Kaliningrad, the Russian Foreign Ministry released a statement through three of its European embassies, warning that Russia is "ready to use all its arsenal, including nuclear weapons, to defend its territory if NATO countries try to isolate Kaliningrad." Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov later explained that this warning was worded in a manner that would "remind those hotheads in Europe" of Russia's long-established conditions for the use of nuclear weapons. Whether for domestic reasons, or because Tusk genuinely perceives a threat from Kaliningrad, these words have fallen on deaf ears in Poland. "In general, the Poles are prone to provoking situations, escalating tensions," Peskov remarked in August. Less than a month later, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov warned in stark terms where escalation could lead. "If the West attacks us, we will respond and it would be a completely different war and a very short one," he said.
